TO the head of a Long Island construction union, the state's proposed $800 million bond act is "like plasma to us, we're dying." But a lawmaker from Nassau County contends that voters are being "sold a bill of goods."

"They say it's going to jump start the economy, but it barely gets the keys out of our pocket," the legislator, Assemblyman Michael Balboni, Republican of Garden City, said. "Jobs should be our No. 1 priority, but we do not have to have a bond to create them."

The Vancouver summit meeting, the $1.6 billion in assistance President Clinton promised President Boris Yeltsin and the decision by 19 Western nations to give Russia 10 more years to pay off $15 billion in debt coming due this year form the first stage of a renewed Western effort to support democratic reforms. 

Much more needs to be done, fast. To stabilize their economy, the Russians will need direct financial assistance of $12 billion a year for the next two years, plus even further debt relief, from the West.

An index of manufacturing in New York state has unexpectedly plummeted, showing the first contraction since 2003 and kindling debate about whether the United States economy is in a period of sluggish growth.

A PROPOSED Metropolitan Transportation Authority capital plan that includes $1.1 billion for the Long Island Rail Road is in jeopardy because of the lagging economy, raising the chances of service cuts.

L.I.R.R. officials said the money, which would help replace aging diesel locomotives and keep the system and its equipment in good repair, may make the difference between improved service and performance or a new era of deferred maintenance and breakdowns.

IN THE DINING ROOM OF THE SUN SPA hotel, Lucky Kargo, a broad-shouldered man with an 88-key grin, is gingerly twirling a fragile woman in a cornflower blue dress. A former Broadway dancer and B-movie actor, Kargo, 70, is clearly restraining himself. But when he tosses his head back for a big stage laugh, his partner, well into her 80's, adjusts her glasses and smiles up at him lovingly. "They like that sexy man appeal," Kargo later confides.

The exchange will be repeated countless times this evening throughout the South Florida world of Latin and ballroom dancing. It's an economy driven by the presence of elderly women: housewives, bank tellers, managers of family real estate, society grande dames, ranging from their 60's to their 90's, who have come to dispel winter. They take the dance lessons that the Sun Spa, like many local hotels, offers its residents during the day. Every night there is dining and dancing. For a $6 fee, a woman can rent a male partner for a two-minute dance -- a chance, however momentary, to scintillate.

Providing this service are men like Kargo: suave, gentlemanly ballroom dancers, age 20 to 85, who know how to play the part of Fred Astaire. Of the $6 paid to the hotel concessionaire, Kargo pockets $3.60 and hopes for tips. (He has since moved on to higher-paying venues.) If the band plays fast, escorts can squeeze 15 or 20 dances into an evening. They hand out business cards to attract private clients. They also attend charity functions for $150 to $200 a night. An hourlong dance lesson at home usually runs $60. "But no hanky-panky," Kargo says.
'Signals Mixed' for Rates

A heavier-than-normal supply of Treasury notes and bonds over the next month could cause interest rates to rise, but credit market analysts are deeply divided about whether an increase in rates could be sustained in coming months.   Recent economic statistics have been ambiguous enough to support a variety of interest rate forecasts. One group maintains that the economy is still sluggish, and that interest rates are likely to decline later this year. Others expect an economic rebound from the 1 percent growth rate of the first half, to a healthier growth rate of 4 percent accompanied by rising interest rates.
A Bank on the Move

The Inter-American Development Bank's principal function is to help the economies of Latin American countries by lending them money. Now, the organization is expected to help the economy of downtown Washington without lending a dime.
A Bind for the Fed

The March trade figures, which will be announced in Washington on Tuesday, are likely to continue the familiar saga of huge merchandise imports and anemic exports for the United States.   Raymond T. Dalio, president of Bridgewater Associates, an economic consulting firm, predicts a merchandise trade deficit of over $12 billion for March, a bit higher than February's $11.5 billion.   But more worrisome, said Mr. Dalio, is a link between the trade deficit and possible moves by the Federal Reserve Board to take the economy out of the doldrums. ''What makes the rising merchandise trade deficit particularly disturbing,'' he said, ''is that the inflow of less- expensive foreign goods is encouraging consumers to take on enormous installment debt burdens.''
A Bond Strategy for Foreigners

LEAD: With the economy slowing down, or possibly in a recession, and with a steadily weakening dollar, there is little to attract foreign investors to the American stock and bond markets From January through May, foreigners were net sellers of $6.7 billion in American stocks and $5.9 billion in Government securities, according to the most recent data from the Securities Industry Association.
A DECENT REPSPECT

WASHINGTON A strong new American policy has   been evolving toward the ''third   world.''   The new way was found with LOST, the most apt acronym of the postwar era - the Law of the Sea Treaty, a grab for the natural resources of the next century by the politicians representing the most backward and totalitarian nations.    The Reagan Administration refused to sign LOST because it did not want the U.S. to become a party to the socialization of the sea, setting up an unaccountable and self-perpetuating world bureaucracy dedicated to regulating and taxing free enterprise.   The decision to turn back from the brink of LOST infuriated the devotees of world government. Denunciations of our ''lawlessness'' came from the back seats of limousines with diplomatic license plates everywhere, and liberal establishmentarians here excoriated the decision to put our national self-interest and principles of a free economy ahead of ''world opinion.''
A Firm Faith in Lower Rates

The Federal Reserve is not expected to change monetary policy at this week's meeting of the Federal Open Market Committee, but many credit market participants remained optimistic last week that interest rates may decline in the near future.   The predisposition in favor of lower interest rates was shown on Friday, when traders and investors shrugged off a Commerce Department report of stronger-than-expected gains in employment. Normally, a 414,000 rise in nonfarm payrolls, plus a strong increase in manufacturing employment, would have led to lower bond prices as analysts concluded that a stronger economy would bring stronger credit demands and discourage the Fed from any further easing in monetary policy.   But on Friday the sharp price declines registered after release of the employment statistics were quickly recouped, and bond prices ended the day with modest gains. ''There was heavy, broad-based buying when prices fell in the morning,'' said one Government securities dealer. ''You don't expect the market to trade up in the face of heavy supply and bad economic news,'' he said. ''But I have to believe the evidence, which is that there was good demand last week.''
A Heartfelt CryFrom AlfonsinOn Debt Crisis

Congress heard from an expert last week about Latin's America's debt problems and the threat they pose to peace and stability in the hemisphere. Far from being abstract, the warning by President Raul Alfonsin of Argentina concerned the survival of civilian democracy in his country.    Mr. Alfonsin's address to a joint meeting came at the end of a three- day visit to Washington in search of aid. Argentina's economy has failed to meet promises made to the International Monetary Fund in September in return for $1.7 billion in loans. Inflation was supposed to fall to a monthly average of 14 percent but in January it was at 25 percent. The country owes $45 billion to foreign creditors and is in arrears on $800 million of interest payments to commercial banks. After disbursing $500 million, the I.M.F has withheld further payments until new terms are set with a negotiating team, which is due in Buenos Aires tomorrow. In the meantime, Argentina is reportedly seeking $500 million as a ''bridging'' loan from the United States, but the Administration has barred any help until Argentina makes its economic reforms effective. Commercial banks are also holding up some $4 billion in loans because of the country's noncompliance with the I.M.F. program. In lieu of money, Mr. Alfonsin had to settle for an honorary degree from New York University, a citation from Columbia University and a medal from the Pan American Society during a visit to New York.
A LEADER WITH STYLE-AND IMPATIENCE

Coming to power at the age of 54, Mikhail Sergeyevich Gorbachev, the peasant's son from southern Russia, is expected to bring a new style of leadership to the Kremlin. If the expectations prove correct, this leadership will be more open, perhaps, less obsessively suspicious, less burdened with memories of Stalin's terror and the war.    For the moment, Mr. Gorbachev seemed anxious to give fire to the program of economic change he had inherited from his mentor, Yuri V. Andropov.    He revealed his impatience in a major speech last December when he said, ''We will have to carry out profound transformations in the economy and in the entire system of social relations.''
A SHARP RISE IN BOND PRICES

Bond prices rose sharply yesterday, as a spate of weak economic data led many traders and investors to conclude that the Federal Reserve will promote lower interest rates in the future.   Even though the Fed made no overt moves to encourage lower rates yesterday, market participants were optimistic that the central bank will resort to an easier monetary policy in order to stimulate the economy.   That optimism was translated into increases of more than one point for Treasury issues due in 10 years or more, with the 11 1/4 percent Treasury issue due in 2015 offered late in the day at 106 6/ 32, to yield 10.56 percent. The price of the bellwether Treasury bond slipped from a late afternoon high of about 106 3/8, because the Federal Reserve did not announce a cut in the discount rate.
A STUBBORN PLATEAU IN THE JOBLESS RATE

Unemployment remained flat for the fifth month at 7.2 percent overall, and the manufacturing segment, which lost 45,000 jobs, continued to take the blame. The figures were a bit of a setback to a resurgent economy. Without a big surge of jobs in manufacturing, economists say, the economy cannot truly recover. In addition, ''There seems to be a shift out of lower-paying occupations into higher-paying occupations,'' said Janet L. Norwood, the commissioner of the Bureau of Labor Statistics. Some economists say that means workers who might have filled manufacturing jobs are being shut out of the job market altogether. And that, they note, may mean that unemployment much below 7 percent will be unattainable.   But other data were promising. Factory orders rebounded 2.1 percent in May, after three months of declines. . . . Spending on new construction rose 1.5 percent in May, and sales of new homes rose 9.7 percent.
A STUDY OF FOOD BUYERS REVEALS SHIFTS IN TASTES

For more than a decade the Food Marketing Institute has been tracking the major trends and attitudes of supermarket shoppers. The surveys, called Trends, conducted by Louis Harris & Associates for the trade association of the wholesale and retail segments of the food industry, offer a comprehensive overview of the changes that have taken place in the last 11 years. Comparing the findings of the first study in 1974 with this year's shows how the public's concerns have shifted.   This year, the generally upbeat mood of the country in 1985 is expressed not only in the attitudes of the 1,005 people surveyed, but also in how they have altered their shopping habits. This year, 51 percent said they believed that the economy would continue to improve. In 1974, 71 percent said things were either pretty bad or fairly bad.

A True Value For the Dollar

THE fall of the dollar in the past two weeks has shaken financial markets throughout the world. What is the dollar really worth - or, as the economists would put it, at what level will it reach a stable equilibrium? Will it get there gradually, making a so-called smooth landing, with benign effects on this country's industries and agriculture that have been hurt by an overvalued dollar, or will it plummet to a crash landing, with serious damage to the United States and the international economy?   There are two key questions: How far has the dollar to come down? And how long will it take to get there?   On the first question, in a world of floating exchange rates, with changing differentials among nations in rates of growth, inflation, wages and interest rates, nobody can know just where equilibrium between the dollar and other currencies will be found.
A Turnaround in Bond Prices

Bond prices rebounded yesterday on fresh evidence of weakness in the economy.   The credit markets, which were depressed Thursday by a surge in the money supply, were bolstered yesterday by the Government report that housing construction fell 2.4 percent in July.   Prices on long-term Government bonds gained 1 1/4 points, more than making up for Thursday's losses. Short-term interest rates drifted moderately lower.

WITH the economy finally showing signs of improvement, the investment community is busily devising scenarios to take advantage of a hoped-for revival in the stock market.   ''Our brokerage firm is recommending defensive food stocks on one hand and sharply depressed technology issues on the other,'' a securities analyst said at midweek. ''I must admit, it all sounds somewhat contradictory.''   On Friday, at least, it was not a bad idea to own food-processing stocks - a group that has scored steady gains over the last several years, thanks not only to growing profits but also to several giant-sized takeovers.
AS ECONOMY FALLS, SO DOES THE DOLLAR

The dollar has been falling as traders worry about the United States economy. The dollar had already hit yearlong lows when President Reagan's illness further depressed it. News of the slowing American economy did little to help the currency, although it recovered some in late-week trading. The drop in the dollar makes American goods cheaper abroad and could help the nation's record trade deficit. But Paul A. Volcker, the chairman of the Federal Reserve, does not want the dollar to fall too far, because it would hurt the Federal deficit as foreign investors withdrew funds.   In Italy, the lira lost 20 percent of its value against the dollar Friday, and the European Monetary System will meet in emergency session to try to stabilize it.
ASHOULD FARMERS BEAR SHARE OF BUDGET CUTS?

Of all the legislation facing Congress this year, none better captures the conflict between fiscal and social pressures than the new farm law that Congress hopes to pass by Christmas.   The debate over the farm bill, which will govern the farm economy for the balance of the decade, has become a contest between the will to reduce Federal budget deficits and the will to help farmers remain on the farm.   At issue is whether farmers should share the burden of deficit reduction along with other beneficiaries of Federal spending, or whether the rest of the economy should pay for reducing the deficits before the Government removes the farmers' cushion.   A bipartisan majority in the House of Representatives has passed a five-year renewal of the 1981 farm law, 282 to 141, about enough votes to override a Presidential veto. The Republican-controlled Senate is debating a bill the Administration finds even more objectionable.
AUTHORS AS ACTORS: THE PLAY'S NOT THE ONLY THING

QUESTION: What do Athol Fugard, Harold Pinter, Sam Shepard, John Osborne, Wallace Shawn, Harvey Fierstein, Christopher Durang, David Mamet, John Pielmeier, Michael Cristofer, Samm-Art Williams and Miguel Pinero have in common? Answer: They are all actors. Of course they are also playwrights, but each of them has earned some if not most of his income by acting on the professional stage or in films, often in his own works. Some, such as Mr. Pinter and Mr. Osborne, were actors before they were playwrights. Others have taken up acting later in their careers, as a matter of economy or opportunity.   Mr. Fugard has been touring with his play ''The Blood Knot,'' re-creating the role he first played a quarter of a century ago in South Africa. The revival opens on Broadway next month. Mr. Pinter, the actor, has returned to the stage in his play ''Old Times,'' opposite Liv Ullmann and Nicola Pagett. By the end of the season, ''Old Times'' may also be on Broadway.

BEHIND THE BROWNSTONE DOOR

Edith Wharton in her memoirs speaks of the New York of her childhood, in the 1870's, as having been ''cursed with the universal chocolate-colored coating of the most hideous stone ever quarried.'' She compared its gridiron uniformity unfavorably with the noble parks and fountained squares that she had seen in contemporaneous Paris and Rome, whither her parents, in those happier days, used periodically to retreat in the interests of economy. But in my own childhood, half a century later, I had not the advantage of the European contrast, which may have been why I viewed my brownstone environment - and I had lived in three such houses - with different eyes.

BOND PRICES CONTINUE TO GAIN

Bond prices continued their advance yesterday on forecasts of slower economic growth.   Although the credit markets are still digesting the heavy supply of Government securities auctioned this week, traders were relieved that the Treasury refinancing was over, and quickly shifted their attention back to the economy. Jones, economist at Aubrey G. Lanston & Company.
BUDGET PLAN STIRS RATE HOPES

Bond market participants hope that the Congressional budget plan announced late Friday will lead to lower interest rates, but many expect that developments in the economy will prevent a quick drop in rates. House and Senate conferees reached an agreement on reducing Federal budget deficits.   Anticipation of a plan to narrow the deficits was an important element in the recent rally in the bond market, which cut the yield on 30-year Treasury bonds to less than 10 percent for the first time since June 1980, down from 10.51 percent as recently as Oct. 28. But the decline in rates has faltered recently, and signs of a healthy economy have caused some analysts to doubt that the Federal Reserve will soon push rates lower by easing monetary policy.
Baldrige's Antitrust Campaign

Secretary of Commerce Malcolm Baldrige has stepped out alone on a couple of issues, such as his proposal to merge the Commerce Department and the special trade representative's office, and they have gotten nowhere. But he may be making headway with his campaign to relax the antitrust laws.   Mr. Baldrige argues that the antitrust laws are antiquated in that they were written to protect consumers from price-fixing and other monopolistic abuses in the largely insular American economy of the early 1900's. But American companies now compete in a much bigger world market, he says, and foreign competitors, with easy access to the American market, serve as a check against such practices.

Bond Prices Advance Sharply

Bond prices rose sharply yesterday as traders and investors began to anticipate that two of the bond markets worst enemies - huge Federal budget deficits and high inflation -are at major turning points and may be less of a threat in the future.   By late in the day, the bellwether 9 7/8 percent Treasury bonds due in 2015 were offered at 101 18/32, up 1 11/32, to yield 9.71 percent. Gains were large for other note and bonds, with the 9 1/8 percent notes due in 1991 rising 5/8 point to an offered price of 100 22/32 to yield 8.95 percent.   ''The market just turned on a dime, and all the concerns last week about a stronger economy and rapid money supply growth leading to higher rates were promptly forgotten,'' said one Treasury note trader who asked not to be identified.
Bond Prices Little Changed

Bond prices were little changed yesterday as the credit markets calmed after the tumultuous tumble in prices on Thursday.   Analysts said the markets had apparently adjusted to a view that the economy was actually much stronger than previously thought and that the improved outlook dampened the prospect for any change in Federal Reserve policy.   ''The fact that the domestic economy is doing so well precludes the Fed from easing credit,'' said Robert J. Christian, director of economic research at the Provident National Bank in Philadelphia. He added that, with no major economic indicators due out until next month, the credit markets should hold relatively steady over the next few weeks.
Bond Prices Resume Advance

After four days of flat to slightly lower prices, the rally in the Treasury securities market resumed yesterday, as dealers reported heavy demand at the early afternoon auction of $7.5 billion in new five-year notes.   By late in the day, the new 9 1/8 percent notes, due Feb. 15, 1991, were offered with a yield of about 9.12 percent, for a slight improvement from the average yield of 9.13 percent set at the auction. The yield for the new five-year issue, which the Treasury auctions quarterly, was the lowest since the auction of April 1978, and was well below the 9.62 percent average for a similar issue auctioned in late August.   Although there is no consensus view among economists about the strength of the economy and direction of interest rates, many traders and investors have been buying notes and bonds in anticipation of lower rates.

Budget Battle Spatters Politicians

WASHINGTON - As the Federal budget deficit threatens to choke the economy, the most powerful men in Government, meeting week after week, hour after hour, have found it far easier to bash each other for inaction than to find common ground.   Faced with a widespread shutdown of Government offices and activities in the absence of a budget agreement, Congress has scheduled sessions for today to revise the deadlines of the Federal budget-balancing law to avoid automatic multi-billion dollar program cuts on Monday. After a compromise between White House and Congressional negotiators late Friday night, it appeared the way was open for a deal that would keep the Government functioning.   But in an atmosphere of growing disgust at debacles such as the savings and loan collapse and the ethical missteps on Capitol Hill, the budget quagmire is for many Americans the most telling evidence yet that the nation's leaders are sacrificing the public interest for their own.   "The mood is almost 100 percent 'the hell with them all,' " said Larry King, the national radio and television call-in host. "I don't remember any time quite like this. Out of 300 calls in the last two weeks, 130 have been on Congress and the deficit. I haven't gotten one call that George Bush is correct and Congress is wrong, or that Congress is correct and George Bush is wrong. There's a 'damn both thy houses' attitude."   Some politicians are equally harsh, among them Representative Lee Hamilton of Indiana. "The most serious consequence of the budget deficit may be that we've lost our credibility," said Mr. Hamilton, one of the most respected House Democrats. "No party, no leader, no member is going to come out of this looking very good. We're letting the country down."   Much of the country would seem to agree. A recent New York Times/CBS News poll showed that 59 percent of those surveyed said they did not believe that President Bush and Congressional leaders were making a serious effort to reduce the deficit. Only about half that number said Mr. Bush and Congress were really making a serious effort.   In follow-up interviews last week, poll respondents said they were fed up like never before. "They're just fighting each other on the news," said Merry Snyder, a 57-year-old care worker for the developmentally disabled in Arlington, Washington. "They're not putting the American people first. They're putting themselves first. They're not thinking about us at all." Wanda Johnston, an 84-year-old retired real estate broker in Phoenix, said that Congress and the White House don't seem "even interested in trying" to remedy the deficit. "They are simply sitting there like two dogs fighting over a bone."   That's the way it seemed last week. Mr. Bush started the latest round of recriminations as he traveled to high-roller Republican fund-raising gatherings in the Middle West warning that if automatic spending cuts take effect Monday, "the Democratic Congress knows that it will be held accountable."   The Democratic Congress was furious. Brandishing a milk carton on the House floor, Representative Bob Wise, a West Virginia Democrat, mocked the President for staying out of Washington at a crucial time in the talks. He said: "There is a face that is soon going to be appearing on the grocery shelves if he does not get back to Washington pretty soon. Come home, President Bush. Call a toll-free number. We will pick you up. Get to the summit where you belong!"   It was not supposed to happen this way. To harness the massive Reagan-era deficits, Congress in 1985 passed the Gramm-Rudman-Hollings law, which called for steady reductions in red ink. Each year since then, Congress and the White House negotiated, only to wind up with a compromise that put off tough decisions for yet another year through budgetary tricks like revising the deficit reduction targets.   This year, with the economy appearing on the brink of recession, the stakes were even higher. But both sides remained adamant in their opposition over one issue in particular, Mr. Bush's proposal to lower the capital gains tax. It was an issue more of symbol than substance - many economists say it would have only a minor impact on the deficit -but it was anathema to Democrats, who note that it benefits mainly the wealthy, and unwaveringly demanded by Mr. Bush, perhaps to ease the pain of his broken pledge of no new taxes. In a compromise late Friday night, the Democrats yielded on capital gains and the White House agreed to a higher income tax for wealthy Americans.   No matter what the final package is, the deficit is not about to disappear. There are no quick fixes in the world of budget making. Senator Warren B. Rudman, a New Hampshire Republican and an author of the deficit-reduction law, suggests that the American system of Government is the core problem.   "I really wonder whether we have reached a stage in our history where the three branches of Government are really working any more," he said. "It's getting to be a formula for gridlock with no accountability, with the American people not knowing whether to blame the President, the Republicans, the Democrats or just everybody."   Of course, if the backroom budget talks result in a breakthrough, it probably won't take long for the warring factions to close ranks: Mr. Bush and Congressional leaders will no doubt gather under bright television lights at the White House to congratulate each other, proclaiming that they have saved the country from what some commentators call "Beltway Armageddon."   For a while, at least, praise will substitute for the back-biting. But it is unlikely to be genuine. As Representative Jim Lightfoot, an Iowa Republican, put it in a tongue-lashing he delivered from the House floor last week:   "I would suggest to my colleagues that many Republicans and good conservative Democrats are sick and tired of being cast and forced into the role of playing the clown. It is time that this circus closed and left town."   THE NATION

The economic forecast for New York City is mostly sunny, State Comptroller Edward V. Regan said last week. In a report prepared for the State Financial Control Board, which has overseen the city's finances since the fiscal crisis of the mid-1970's, Mr. Regan said that New York's economy is stronger now than at any other time in the past 25 years, and that steady growth is likely to continue.
Business-Form Outlook Bright

WHILE computer manufacturers are mired in a virtual recession, the business-forms industry is enjoying a boom. In a sense, Wall Street analysts say, this phenomenon reflects the split personality of the economy.   Small, service-related industries are riding the crest of good times. But the broad manufacturing sector - including technology - faces such negatives as oversupply, intensifying competition and a strong dollar.
C.D.'s, Money Funds Show a Slight Increase

Rates on certificates of deposit and money market mutual funds rose slightly for the week ended yesterday, while bank money market accounts continued to hold steady.   Analysts remain divided over the propects of interest rates. Some contend that recently released economic data point to the economy picking up steam, which could be followed by a rise in rates. Others, however, contend that the elements for sustained economic recovery are still lacking.
CAVIAR, GENERAL?

A COUPLE OF HEAVY-weight professors were sparring recently on the ''CBS Morning News'' about the wisdom of the nuclear shield called ''Star Wars.'' I was in bed in a hotel room, getting a second reprieve from a snooze alarm, when I heard the voice of Arthur M. Schlesinger Jr., a Distinguished Professor of the City University of New York (who happens also to be a distinguished professor, uncapitalized, in real life). He was knocking the President's plan, which did not interrupt my reverie, but then he said something about ''not helping the sclerotic economy.''   Moments later, Prof. Richard E. Pipes of Harvard, a Star Wars enthusiast, picked up the word, perhaps ironically, and talked of ''the sclerotic economy of the Soviet Union.'' I sat up, smacked the snooze alarm again (snooze strikes me as a marriage of snore and doze, but the word has been drifting off since 1788) and waited for the interviewer to ask ''Wait a minute - what does sclerotic mean?''   She did not. Maria Shriver, an intelligent reporter, is not yet secure enough to admit ignorance of a word. Come to think of it, I have never heard any commentator or reporter say ''That's an interesting word - what does it mean?'' Unity Approaches, and East Germany Is Looming Smaller

BONN - IT has become common to speak of German unity in somber and elevated tones, as befits an event of such indisputable historic dimensions. But it is also instructive to note that the actual moment of unity, Oct. 3, was selected not for any historic or symbolic significance, but as a result of the most rollicking variety of political maneuvering.   Chancellor Helmut Kohl came to realize that unity was likely to create considerable dislocation and sacrifice on both sides, so he began pressing for reunification and elections as quickly as possible, before the full cost of the process began to undermine his aura as the Unity Chancellor. The opposition Social Democrats, for similar reasons, began demanding an even earlier date for unity - so that Mr. Kohl could be held directly responsible for any nastiness - and a later date for elections.   The struggle went through much of the summer, with both sides drawing heavily on military imagery to describe their successes and losses. When the Social Democrats succeeded in keeping the election in December, they spoke of "occupying an important strategic height" and of demonstrating "that we can stop the elephant Kohl." The Christian Democrats fought back with speeches accusing the Social Democratic front-runner of "hoping that the people in East Germany will be worse off so that his election chances would rise."   The maneuvering lasted through most of July and August, until finally the politicians agreed to merge the Germanys on Oct. 3, the earliest date possible for external reasons, and to hold state elections in East Germany on Oct. 14, followed by the first all-German balloting on Dec. 2.   What this means is that Oct. 3 will effectively mark the start of the final round in what must rank as one of the most hectic years in modern German politics.   Posters have already appeared around Bonn showing Mr. Kohl with the slogan, "Chancellor for Unity." At the same time, carpetbagging West German politicians have fanned through East Germany to run for the new vacancies there.   In the most celebrated such race, Kurt Biedenkopf, a former secretary general of the West German Christian Democrats who fell afoul of Mr. Kohl, is running for governor of Saxony against Anke Fuchs, the party manager of the West German Social Democrats.   It will be for history to judge whether the handling of unity has been wise or foolish. Ultimately, there may have been no real alternative to the headlong rush of the the last year; once the Berlin Wall was breached on Nov. 9 - and no German politician can claim credit for that - it became largely a question of managing what was effectively an accomplished fact.   Still, the cracking of the wall also sounded the starting gong for a political free-for-all in which nothing - not the date of unity, not economic union - has been left "above politics." Mr. Kohl, the consummate clubhouse pol, has so far proved himself the more adept player, pushing unity through a maze of political, economic and social obstacles with extraordinary energy and resourcefulness. By all current barometers, he appears certain to win the balloting in December to become the first elected chancellor of the reunited Germany.   Many have criticized the politicking as unseemly. Commentators in West Germany and abroad have lamented what one termed the hijacking of a solemn historic moment by a rowdy election campaign.   Yet there are those who argue that the politicians have not done so badly. Despite the extraordinary pace of unification and the disintegration of the East German economy, politicians and officials in both West and East have managed the administrative takeover so far without serious glitches.   "For anyone who has witnessed over the past 15 years the months of struggles over minor problems, this has been proof of a totally unexpected soundness," wrote Hans-Peter Schwarz, director of the political science department at the University of Bonn. "One of the many surprising discoveries of the past nine months is that West Germany, in the federal government and the states, has very competent politicians and officials."   One charge, heard most often from the rump of the East German Communist party, restyled the Party of Democratic Socialism, and from the popular movements that led the mass demonstrations in East Germany last fall, is that the West German politicians have essentially run over East Germany, shoving aside everything indigenous, including fledgling popular movements like New Forum.   Nobody denies the degree to which the West German parties have taken over in East Germany. But that is hardly surprising, according to Josef Joffe, foreign editor of the Suddeutsche Zeitung, who is now a visiting professor at Harvard University.   "The West is essentially taking over a moribund company, and insists on running it," he said. "So it's natural that some East Germans feel they escaped from an indigenous totalitarian regime only to slip into the clutches of an imported regime that's running them 'for their own good'."   The Western dominance, however, cannot last for long, and the East German electorate is certain to eventually define its own interests. The question then will be what shape it gives to the politics of a unified Germany.   One line of speculation is that the addition of 16 million Protestants and a region with strong socialist traditions could shift the balance away from the Christian Democrats and their conservative Bavarian allies the Christian Socialists, and give new strength to the Social Democrats.   But initial voting patterns in East Germany have suggested that 40 years of Communism have fostered an allergy to socialism in any form and that religious differences are no longer as strong as they once were. So far, in any case, the Christian Democrats have shown the greater strength in the East.   A stronger possibility is that Germany will become divided along rich-poor lines, with a struggling East pitted against a protective West. One initial indication of this was the decision by West Germany to give its large states greater weight in the upper house of Parliament, enough to deny the five new East German states a collective veto.   Even longer-term prognoses divide Germany into a rich south - with a revived industrial belt in Saxony in East Germany shaping a "green belt" with the rich West German southern states of Badem-Wurttemberg and Bavaria - and a poor north. Agriculture and industry are suffering in both East and West Germany.  One effect that is already apparent has been the battering of fringe parties on both right and left. In West Germany, the right-wing Republican Party has disintegrated in internal squabbling and the far right has found no new cause around which to rally.   On the left, the Party of Democratic Socialism - the restyled East German Communists - have rallied under their chairman, Gregor Gysi, to form a nationwide alliance of the left. Current opinion polls, however, do not give them the five percent needed to enter Parliament, and their net effect may be to siphon critical votes from the Greens.   If these trends persist, the first Parliament elected by a unified Germany is likely to consist largely of major parties with Mr. Kohl's coalition again in the saddle. Current polls show Mr. Kohl's Christian Democrats with 45 percent, followed by the Social Democrats, with 36 percent. That would leave Mr. Kohl once again dependent on Foreign Minister Hans-Dietrich Genscher's Free Democrats, with about 10 percent of the vote, to form a coalition government. Capitalitis is like that, with the current symptoms not at all unlike those seen in the last century when the press echoed the complaints of aides of another President about their boss's distracting habit of telling anecdotes and making quips, a press also aching for a leader who was more in tune with themselves and the capital culture, who saw the "complexities" of governing -- someone like, say, George McClellan.   So just as pragmatism wasn't vision, journalism ain't history. The Eastern Europeans, with an unsurpassed clinical experience in the field, welcome Mr. Reagan as the man who took a saber to Communism. Former Reagan aides like Caspar Weinberger, Martin Anderson and Constantine Menges have written accounts in which Mr. Reagan emerges as engaged, persistent and intellectually formidable. Lest there be any confusion, let it be understood right now that the family by the name of Crowther, which is principally involved in the British film, "Master of Bankdam," is not related to the writer of this review. At least, we have no personal knowledge of any consanguinity with the clan of Yorkshire woollen mill folk who are saliently displayed in this film. That is an affirmation that you will appreciate, we feel sure, as you learn more about this solemn saga that came to the Embassy Forty-second Street on Saturday.For he simple fact is that the Crowthers to whom we are here introduced are a pretty tight lot of enterprisers, with more than one viperous character in the clan. The mean ones are grasping and deceitful, full of pomposity and guile, and even the nice ones are given to a cheerless probity. More than that, they are rigidly addicted to long hours of hard work at low pay, which is probably the most revolting disposition that they reveal.But once these gloomy characteristics are reflected upon impersonally, then this "Master of Bankdam" emerges as a somberly fascinating tale of a family's internal frictions through three generations and fifty years. And once these crusty Crowthers are accepted as likely Yorkshire types, their struggles for wealth and position become dourly interesting.Not that they or their doings are very different, in basic respects, from the characters or the happenings in any number of other tales of the rise and fall of families in an expanding industrial age. The father, the first of the mill-owning family, is a conventionally autocratic type, endowed with the usual peasant virtues and a solid commercial point of view. He runs his small mill in Yorkshire with the same shrewd economy that he and his wife, a workman's daughter, run their modest home.And his two sons are equally conventional. One is a bright and diligent lad, given to open-handed dealing, and the other is a cold and treacherous drudge. Likewise, the wives of these brothers run pretty true to form; the wife of the first is a darling, the wife of the second is a shrew. There are obvious complications—rivalries, double-crosses, deaths—and a natural continuation of the contention to the sons of the sons. In the end, the family's hard-earned fortunes are saved from disaster and ruin by the son of the good son taking over from the fat-headed son of the bad.As we say, it is all quite familiar, in a flowing Galsworthian vein, and at times it is also quite tedious as the episodes tend to repeat. But happily the producers have set it in a solid atmosphere of a nineteenth century mill town and Victorian society. And a cast of competent actors, under the direction of Walter Forde, play the Yorkshire people with style and authority.Tom Walls is exceptionally forceful as the father of the clan, agitating and aging with drive and integrity. Dennis Price is fluent as the good son, Stephen Murray is bitter as the bad and Nancy Price gives a sure performance as the hard-grained mother of the lads. Anne Crawford and Linden Travers are distinctive as the wives, and Jimmy Hanley and David Tomlinson colorfully portray their sons.We don't want to recommend these Crowthers as the most illustrious bearers of the name, but we've got to admit—these Bankdam mill people make a round and eventful tale.

'Something Askew' In Society's Contrasts

The Oct. 21 issue was a puzzlement in contrasts. The front-page lead article was headlined "New Homes for Lives of Luxury Late in Life" and dealt with the growing older group of New Jersey citizens who are retiring to luxurious surroundings and the developing industry catering to them.   The Opinion page had an article with the headline "Spending a Night With the Homeless" and a subtitle, "The people at a shelter aren't so different from us."   Also on the front page was "S.& L.  Crisis Hurting State's Economy." This article emphasized the difficulty that potential borrowers are having in borrowing funds in excess of 100 percent collateral.   I read this and learned that borrowers and bankers alike seemed to think such loans were not out of line since deposits were insured by the Federal Savings and Loan Insurance Corporation for up to $100,000. No need for the bank to be careful.   What a confusing, unsettling grouping of articles. What a sad commentary on our present society. Are we really very much like, very close to the homeless? Who are those who live "lives of luxury late in life" who are so great in number as to create a whole new industry in the state?   And who are those who are borrowing from the banks in excess of 100 percent of their collateral? Is it right to make loans in excess of collateral and rely on the taxpayer to take up the risk such a loan involves?   There is enough food for thought here to last a lifetime. Who are we really most like? The luxury-living retirees? The high-flying borrowers? The homeless? Which is representative of our society? Do we have a "good" society when there are such extreme contrasts, where credit is so loosely provided?   If nothing else, one must at least recognize that such dramatically contrasting conditions and points of view cannot lead to a stable society or economy. There is something askew in New Jersey as well as the rest of our country.   Will we recognize this? Will we do something to correct it? Or will we wait for some calamity to bring us to our senses?  CHARLES P. HUETHER Clifton

'Two or Three Things I Know About Her ...'

In his shock to the cinematic system, shot in 1966 and released the next year, Jean-Luc Godard wanders far and wide over two landscapes, those of Paris and of a young female body. The ''her'' in the film's title is meant to be Paris, which was in the midst of an enormous government modernization initiative. There is, however, another ''her,'' Juliette (Marina Vlady, above), a housewife who regularly travels from the suburbs into the city, where she moonlights as a prostitute. At this point in his filmmaking evolution, Mr. Godard had all but abandoned (demolished might be the truer word) classic narrative cinema in favor of the essayistic, the associative and the analytic. Thus in ''Two or Three Things,'' instead of a specific story (boy meets working girl), he offers us multiple, intersecting, fragmented stories involving gender, language, consumerism, imperialism and the topographies of desire represented by Paris and Juliette. Here, amid splashes of bold color, discordant sound and brilliant observation, the personal meets the political, as the curves of Juliette's body (unusually plump for a Godard actress) find an echo in the soft lines of a city under assault in the name of progress. In a hushed, urgent voice-over, Mr. Godard attacks the plan's nominal idealism, accusing the Gaullist government of using modernism to mask its disruption both of the nation's economy and of its ''moral fiber.'' Last fall, when some of the suburban towns created through this initiative were engulfed in rioting and flames, Mr. Godard's oracular powers seemed particularly acute. The new CinemaScope print of the film makes this perennial must-see a must-see-now. Eileen Simpson's current book, ''Poets in Their Youth,'' gives us some idea of how poets talk to one another, as opposed to the way they talk to themselves and their readers in their poems. Inspired by Mrs. Simpson's recollections, I've been wondering about the conversation between T.S. Eliot and Ezra Pound when Eliot first saw Pound's revision of his rough draft of ''The Waste Land.'' As there is no verbatim record of the occasion, I have ventured to surmise from what we know of each man what he might have said. For purely dramatic reasons and without a shred of evidence, I've assumed that Pound showed Eliot a clean copy of the revised version. *   Eliot: Did I write that?  Pound: Inside every fat poem, there's a lean poem trying to get out.  Eliot: It doesn't even look familiar.  Pound: All I cut was the stage directions and a few talky-pawky passages.  Eliot (reads): Hm! It's awfully dense.  Pound: Well, there's less air in it and more around it.  Eliot: But it was such a nice, big poem.  Pound: Economy is the soul of poetry. In fact, it's the subject of my next poem.  Eliot: How will people read it?  Pound: Who reads? (He laughs boisterously.) It's the things you say, Tom, not what you don't say, that get you into trouble. A poem should be good and tight, because reviewers are like rats -they come in through the holes.

The Government today reported the first official indication that the recession, which began last July, may be over.   The so-called flash estimate of the gross national product in the second quarter shows that the economy grew six-tenths of 1 percent at an annual rate, after adjustment for inflation, according to Commerce Department figures.   This preliminary number, based on incomplete data for the quarter, is the first time that the G.N.P., the broadest measure of the nation's economy, has risen since the July-through-September quarter of last year. Eighth Since World War II   But while the recession, the eighth since World War II and the second in two years, appears to be over, according to the G.N.P.flash estimate, the economy could remain stagnant and the strength of the hoped-for recovery is unclear. This means that the unemployment rate, which was 9.5 percent in May, might not climb much higher, but the hoped-for decline might be some months off.
